headlines.meta_description: YNAB, EveryDollar, Goodbudget, PocketGuard and Honeydue compared: how each budget app works, what it costs and who it suits.
headlines.h1: Best Budget Apps: YNAB, EveryDollar, Goodbudget, PocketGuard and Honeydue Compared

draft.markdown:
The best budget app for most people is YNAB, because it has you give every dollar a job before you spend it, and one subscription covers up to six people. If you'd rather start without paying, EveryDollar and Goodbudget both have free versions, PocketGuard shows what's left to spend after bills, and Honeydue is a free app built for couples.

## Budget apps at a glance

A budget app records your spending and helps you plan where your money goes before the month starts. The five below differ in three ways that decide the choice: the method they use, what they cost after any trial, and whether a partner can share the budget. The table sums up what each app publishes on its own website. Where a site doesn't say, the cell reads "not published".

| App | Budgeting method | Published price | Sharing | Bank sync |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| YNAB | give every dollar a job before you spend | $109 a year or $14.99 a month, plus tax, after a 34-day trial with no credit card (direct sign-up) | one subscription for up to 6 people | connect accounts and import transactions |
| EveryDollar | zero-based | free version with no time limit; premium $79.99 a year or $17.99 a month after a 14-day trial (new users) | household feature: a couple runs one budget with separate sign-ins | premium only |
| Goodbudget | envelope | free plan (10 + 10 envelopes, 1 account, 2 devices); premium $10 a month or $80 a year | syncs a household budget across phones | premium only, US banks |
| PocketGuard | zero-based, 50/30/20, envelope or custom | $74.99 a year, $12.99 a month or $149.99 once, after a 7-day trial | not published | links your accounts |
| Honeydue | not published (a shared view of money for couples) | free app | built for couples; each partner chooses what to share | 20,000+ institutions in 5 countries |

## How we chose these five

We started from what Google showed for "best budget app" on 2026-10-05. People Also Ask names YNAB, and YNAB, EveryDollar, Goodbudget, PocketGuard and Honeydue each appear in at least two of the three ranking roundups we read. Every fact below comes from the app's own website, read the same day. Where a site is silent, we say "not published".

Six of the top 10 results for this search are forum threads, social posts or videos, so readers want to hear from people who use these apps. We read each app's own pages; we did not test the apps for this draft. [ADD: a month of your own use of your top pick, with a screenshot of its budget screen.]

## 1. YNAB: the best budget app for planning every dollar

YNAB is the pick for people who want a method, not only a tracker. You give every dollar a job before you spend it, connect your accounts to import transactions, and set goals for saving and paying off debt. One subscription can be shared with partners, family or a close group of up to six people, which makes it good value for a household.

YNAB costs $109 a year or $14.99 a month, plus tax where it applies. You can try it for 34 days without a credit card when you sign up directly with YNAB, and college students get a 365-day trial. YNAB says it makes money only from subscriptions and doesn't sell your data. [ADD: what your first week of setup was like.]

## 2. EveryDollar: a free zero-based budget with a paid upgrade

EveryDollar suits people who want [zero-based budgeting](https://www.example.com/blog/zero-based-budgeting/) and are happy to enter transactions by hand to keep it free. Its free version has no time limit and lets you build a monthly budget with unlimited categories, track and split transactions manually, set bill due dates and plan sinking funds. It comes from Ramsey and follows the debt snowball method for paying off debt.

Premium adds bank connect, which pulls transactions into your budget, plus payday planning, custom reports, CSV export and coaching. It costs $79.99 a year or $17.99 a month after a 14-day trial for new users. The household feature lets a couple run one budget with separate sign-ins.

## 3. Goodbudget: envelope budgeting you can share

Goodbudget suits households that like the [envelope method](https://www.example.com/blog/envelope-budgeting/): you set money aside in envelopes for rent, groceries or date night and spend from those, not from your account balance. The budget syncs across iPhones and Android phones, so when one person spends from an envelope, the other sees it. It also runs on the web.

The free plan gives you 10 regular and 10 more envelopes, 1 account, 2 devices and a year of history. Premium costs $10 a month or $80 a year and adds automatic bank sync for US banks, unlimited envelopes and accounts, 5 devices, 7 years of history and email support.

## 4. PocketGuard: see what's safe to spend

PocketGuard suits people who mostly want to know what they can still spend this month. Its Leftover view shows how much money remains after necessities, and Pace forecasts what you'll have left at month end from your spending so far. You can budget zero-based, [50/30/20](https://www.example.com/blog/50-30-20-budget-rule/), envelope style or your own way, on the web, iOS, Apple Watch and Android.

It also spots recurring charges so you can cancel subscriptions you forgot, and it builds a debt payoff plan. PocketGuard costs $74.99 a year, $12.99 a month or $149.99 once for lifetime access, after a 7-day trial. It says it shows no ads and doesn't sell data. Sharing a budget with a partner is not published on the pages we read.

## 5. Honeydue: a free money app for couples

Honeydue suits couples who want to see their money together without merging everything. It's a free mobile app for iPhone and Android, and each partner chooses what to share. It tracks bank accounts, loans and investments from more than 20,000 financial institutions across 5 countries, and it reminds you, or your partner, when a bill is due.

You can react to or ask about a transaction in the app's chat. Honeydue doesn't publish a budgeting method such as envelopes or zero-based planning on the pages we read, so treat it as a shared view of your money rather than a full planner.

## How to choose a budget app

Choose the budget app that matches how you like to plan. If you want a strict method and will pay for it, YNAB is the strongest pick here. If you want to start without paying, EveryDollar's free version and Goodbudget's free plan both work with manual entry. If you mainly want to stop overspending, PocketGuard's Leftover view helps.

- **Planning every dollar, shared with family:** YNAB.
- **Zero-based budgeting at no cost:** EveryDollar's free version.
- **Envelope budgeting with a partner:** Goodbudget.
- **Knowing what's safe to spend:** PocketGuard.
- **Seeing money together as a couple:** Honeydue.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the #1 budgeting app?

YNAB is the top pick in this guide, because it gives you a full method for planning every dollar and one subscription covers up to six people. There is no single #1 for everyone, though: if cost matters most, EveryDollar and Goodbudget have free versions, and Honeydue is free for couples. Pick the app whose method you will keep using.

### What is the best free app for budgeting?

EveryDollar's free version is the strongest free option here for planning, because it has no time limit and allows unlimited categories, though you enter transactions by hand. Goodbudget's free plan suits envelope budgeting, with 10 regular and 10 more envelopes on 2 devices. Honeydue is a free app for couples who want to track money together.

### Is YNAB really worth it?

YNAB is worth it if you will follow its method of giving every dollar a job, and the trial is the way to find out. It costs $109 a year or $14.99 a month, but you can try it for 34 days without a credit card when you sign up directly, and one subscription covers up to six people.
